nameStory: The name 'comb-tailed spider' comes from the distinctive row of bristles on the back legs that look like tiny combs. These specialized bristles help the spider manage its unique sheet web, acting like little tools to keep the silken surface taut and organized.
description: Antistea brunnea is a tiny brownish spider that builds horizontal sheet webs close to the ground. These diminutive hunters are part of the comb-tailed spider family, named for their specialized leg bristles. They're quite small, typically less than a quarter-inch in body length, with a modest brown coloration that helps them blend into leaf litter and low vegetation.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Look for delicate horizontal sheet webs stretched between grass stems or low plants, often with a slight funnel or retreat area where the spider waits

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Small, compact spider with a rounded abdomen and relatively long legs for its body size, feeling delicate if gently touched

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Overall brownish coloration ranging from light tan to darker brown, often with subtle darker markings that may appear as faint chevrons or spots

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Body length typically under 6mm (about a quarter-inch), small enough to easily sit on a fingernail with room to spare

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Usually found sitting motionless on or near their sheet web, quickly running to the web's edge when prey gets tangled in the silken surface

habitat: Found in low vegetation areas including meadows, forest edges, and gardens where they can anchor their sheet webs between grass stems and small plants. They prefer areas with some moisture and protection from strong winds, often in spots where leaf litter meets living vegetation.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning to construct their characteristic sheet webs in protected spots among emerging vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when webs are most visible and spiders are actively hunting small flying insects that get caught in their horizontal snares.
seasonality.fall: Mating occurs and egg sacs are produced, though the tiny size makes observation of reproductive behavior challenging for casual observers.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off with hard frosts, while eggs or juveniles overwinter in protected locations under bark or in leaf litter.

funFact: Despite being incredibly tiny, comb-tailed spiders are engineering marvels - they use their specialized leg combs like tiny tools to literally 'comb' their sheet webs, keeping the silk strands perfectly aligned and tensioned for maximum prey-catching efficiency.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small sheet web spiders, but the horizontal orientation of the web and the spider's position on top (rather than underneath) helps distinguish comb-tailed spiders from similar species.
contextualKnowledge: With only one observation recorded in New England, this species appears to be quite rare in our region, making any sighting particularly noteworthy for local spider diversity records.
compareHints: As the only Antistea species in our region, compare it with other comb-tailed spider family members by looking for the horizontal sheet web style. Other Hahniidae species may have different web orientations or retreat structures, and Antistea brunnea tends to be on the smaller end of the size range for this spider family.
